Floating-point addition fails to be associative because floating-point numbers are stored with finite precision—typically 24 bits of mantissa for single precision or 53 bits for double precision—and every arithmetic operation must round its result back to a representable value. When you add two numbers whose magnitudes differ substantially, the smaller number may lose some or all of its significant bits during rounding, since it has to be aligned to the exponent of the larger number before the addition occurs. This means that the result of (a + b) + c can differ from a + (b + c) whenever the intermediate sums have different magnitudes and therefore trigger different rounding decisions. The order in which numbers are combined determines which intermediate values appear, and thus determines what information is discarded to rounding error. Because this is a fundamental consequence of finite representation rather than a hardware defect, it holds on every platform that uses IEEE 754 or similar floating-point formats, though the specific way this non-associativity manifests depends heavily on hardware and software choices.

This becomes especially relevant for large matrix multiplications because each output element is computed as a sum of many products, and that sum is a reduction operation whose order is not fixed by the mathematics of the problem—only by the implementation. Modern hardware introduces many opportunities for the reduction order to vary: GPUs and multi-core CPUs parallelize the summation across many threads, and the order in which partial sums are combined depends on thread scheduling, block sizes, and the specific decomposition of the matrix into tiles. Vectorized instructions (SIMD, AVX, tensor cores) may sum several elements simultaneously using tree-like reduction patterns rather than sequential accumulation, again changing intermediate rounding behavior. Libraries such as BLAS implementations, cuBLAS, or different versions of the same library may choose different blocking strategies or algorithms (e.g., Strassen-like methods) that alter the order of additions. Even running the same code on the same hardware can yield different results if the number of threads changes, since that changes how partial sums are grouped and merged.

As a consequence, the same logical matrix multiplication can produce numerically different results—differing in the last few bits or occasionally more significantly when catastrophic cancellation is involved—depending on the hardware, library version, thread count, or batching strategy used. This creates real challenges for reproducibility in scientific computing and machine learning, where researchers may struggle to exactly replicate results across different GPUs, framework versions, or parallelization settings, even though the underlying mathematical operation is identical.

Floating-point numbers are represented with a finite number of significand bits, so most arithmetic operations must round their true mathematical result to the nearest representable value. This rounding is the root cause of non-associativity. When you compute (a + b) + c, the intermediate sum a + b is rounded to fit the floating-point format before c is added, and that rounded intermediate value then participates in a second rounding when added to c. If you instead compute a + (b + c), a different intermediate value is formed and rounded, and the final result can differ in its last bit or bits from the first grouping. Mathematically, real-number addition is associative, but the rounding step injected between operations breaks this property for floating-point addition. The magnitude and sign of the numbers involved matter a great deal: adding a very small number to a very large one can cause the small number's contribution to vanish entirely due to limited precision, whereas summing several small numbers together first before adding the large one can preserve their combined effect. This sensitivity to ordering means that seemingly trivial changes in how a sum is grouped can produce measurably different results.

This matters enormously for large matrix multiplications because a single output element is the sum of potentially thousands or millions of individual products, and modern hardware computes that sum using highly parallel, tiled, and pipelined execution strategies. GPUs, multi-core CPUs, and specialized accelerators split the reduction across many threads, cores, or vector lanes, and the partial sums are combined in an order that depends on the number of threads, the tile size, the scheduling, and even runtime conditions like which core finishes first. Libraries such as cuBLAS or MKL may choose different algorithms depending on matrix dimensions, hardware generation, or library version, each implying a different summation order. Because floating-point addition is not associative, these different reduction orders can yield results that differ in the least significant bits, and these tiny discrepancies can accumulate through deep neural networks or iterative numerical algorithms, sometimes producing visibly different outcomes after many layers or iterations. As a consequence, running the same matrix multiplication on different hardware, different thread counts, or different library versions can produce bitwise different results even though all computations are performed correctly according to IEEE floating-point rules. This makes strict bitwise reproducibility across platforms difficult to guarantee, and it is why frameworks that require deterministic behavior often need to fix the reduction order explicitly, sometimes at the cost of parallel performance.

Floating-point numbers are a finite subset of the reals: each value is a sign, a fixed-width significand, and an exponent, so only numbers representable in that format can be stored exactly. When two such numbers are added, the exact mathematical sum usually requires more significand bits than the format provides, so the hardware rounds the result to the nearest representable value. That rounding step, not the addition itself, is what destroys associativity. In (a + b) + c the intermediate a + b is rounded before c is added, whereas in a + (b + c) the intermediate b + c is rounded first, and the two roundings generally discard different information. A classic illustration is adding a very large number, its negation, and a small number: if the small value is absorbed into the large one during the first addition it vanishes entirely, while if the two large values cancel first the small value survives intact. Cancellation, absorption of tiny addends into large accumulators, and occasional overflow or underflow all mean that the error depends on the order in which partial sums are formed. Addition remains commutative, since rounding a + b and b + a yields the same result, but grouping matters.

Matrix multiplication is built almost entirely from summation: every output element is a dot product, a reduction over the shared dimension. On modern hardware that reduction is rarely performed as a simple left-to-right loop. Vector units accumulate several partial sums in parallel lanes and combine them at the end, cache-blocked kernels split the inner dimension into tiles whose partial results are added later, multithreaded and GPU implementations assign different ranges of the reduction to different cores or warps and merge them in a tree, and fused multiply-add instructions keep the product at full precision before rounding, which changes the error profile again. Tensor cores and similar units may accumulate in a wider precision than the inputs, or use block-wise accumulation with its own rounding rules. Each of these strategies computes a mathematically identical expression but a numerically different one.

The practical consequence is that the same code, given the same inputs, can produce different results when the thread count changes, when a library picks a different blocking strategy for a different matrix shape, when work is scheduled nondeterministically across GPU blocks, or when the binary is run on a machine with different vector widths. The differences are usually tiny per element, but they can be amplified by ill-conditioned problems, iterative solvers, or long training runs where small divergences compound. Achieving bitwise reproducibility therefore requires deliberately fixing the reduction order, using deterministic library modes, or employing compensated or exactly-rounded summation algorithms, all of which typically cost performance.
